records.source: ISO 24495-1:2023, Plain language, Part 1: Governing principles and guidelines
records.population: Anyone producing documents for a defined readership; drafted by experts from twenty-five countries covering nineteen languages
records.licence: ISO copyright, sold under ISO terms, not open; no reuse of text permitted
records.finding: Plain language is defined by reader outcome, not by text features. A document is plain when the intended readers can find what they need, understand it, and use it. That flips the unit of judgement from the sentence to the task, and it makes plainness a property of a reader-document pair rather than of the prose. The principles are framed around findability, comprehension and usability rather than word counts, so the standard cannot be satisfied by running a formula.
records.applicability_limits: The standard is paywalled and only the public abstract and preview pages were consulted, so the exact normative wording was not read and must not be paraphrased closely. It offers principles, not thresholds: no sentence length, no vocabulary list, no pass mark. It is written for documents, not for interface strings, error text or microcopy, where the reader has no time to study anything. Part 1 is language-agnostic in claim but was drafted mainly from European-language practice.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-07 is a randomised trial where a plain-language rewrite improved satisfaction and usability but did not significantly improve understanding, which is the outcome the standard makes definitional.
records.review: on-change-of:ISO publishing Part 2 or revising Part 1

records.source: Federal Plain Language Guidelines, now hosted as the Digital.gov plain language guide series
records.population: United States federal agencies writing for the public, mandated by the Plain Writing Act of 2010
records.version_or_commit: Digital.gov guide series as published 2026-08-03; plainlanguage.gov now 301-redirects here, with the prior material archived in the PlainLanguage.gov GitHub repository
records.licence: United States federal government work, public domain within the United States; no explicit statement was found on the page itself
records.finding: The guidance splits into four stages that are worth keeping separate: write for understanding, design for understanding, test for understanding, and the legal obligation that creates the duty. The load-bearing move is the third. Plain language is treated as a claim to be tested with real readers, not a style to be asserted, and the guidance carries a statutory hook, so the writing standard has an owner and a consequence.
records.applicability_limits: United States government context. The statutory driver does not exist for private products, so the accountability that makes the guidance stick does not transfer. Aimed at public-facing documents and forms rather than developer-facing or machine-consumed text. The 2026 migration from plainlanguage.gov to digital.gov moved and reorganised the material, so any deep link into the old guidelines is now unreliable.

records.source: GOV.UK, Writing to GOV.UK standards (Government Digital Service publishing guidance)
records.population: UK government content designers publishing to GOV.UK; audience is the whole UK adult population including the lowest literacy band
records.version_or_commit: guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk as published 2026-08-03; migrated in 2025 from www.gov.uk/guidance/content-design, which now 301-redirects
records.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, stated in the site footer as applying except where otherwise stated; attribution to the Government Digital Service required
records.finding: Content is designed against a user need, not a subject. The structural rules are that a page starts from the need, front-loads the answer, and uses the words the reader already uses rather than the words the organisation uses. The famous reading age target is a proxy for a stronger claim: write for the lowest literacy in the audience, because the specialists cope with plain wording and the strugglers do not cope with anything else. Rules for specific words live in a separate A to Z, which is the right shape: principles in one place, arbitrary lexical decisions in a list that can churn without touching the principles.
records.applicability_limits: OGL requires attribution, so lifting the A to Z wholesale into a house guide is a licensing event, not a copy-paste. The guidance is tuned to transactional government information read once under stress; it is a poor fit for developer reference, marketing, or any content where a term of art is genuinely the clearest word. The reading age figure is asserted rather than evidenced on the page, and the underlying literacy statistics are UK-specific. Several deep links into this material broke during the 2025 migration.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-04 shows the readability formulas used to check a reading age are weak predictors of actual difficulty, so the target can be met without the outcome improving.
records.review: on-change-of:GDS restructuring the writing guidelines or the A to Z style guide

records.source: Begeny and Greene, Can readability formulas be used to successfully gauge difficulty of reading materials?
records.study_design: Comparison of eight formula-assigned grade levels for graded passages against measured oral reading fluency rates of the same passages
records.population: 360 elementary-aged students in the United States
records.benchmark: Oral reading fluency rate as the difficulty criterion
records.version_or_commit: Psychology in the Schools, volume 51, issue 2, pages 198 to 215, published February 2014
records.licence: Wiley copyright, paywalled; abstract and secondary reporting only
records.finding: Readability formulas agree with measured reading difficulty only patchily, and where they do agree it is at particular grade bands rather than across the range. The general principle is that formulas measure surface proxies, average sentence length and average syllables, and those proxies are causally downstream of difficulty rather than difficulty itself. That makes a formula usable as a smoke alarm and unusable as an acceptance criterion, because it can be satisfied by shortening sentences without changing what a reader can do.
records.applicability_limits: Children reading aloud, not adults scanning an interface. Oral reading fluency is a proxy for difficulty and not the same construct as comprehension. Only the abstract and secondary reporting were read, so the per-formula results are not recorded here. Nothing in it addresses screen text, microcopy or non-English languages, where the syllable-counting basis of most formulas is meaningless.
records.counter_evidence: The same study reports that a small number of formulas were fairly good indicators at some grade levels, so the finding is that formulas are unreliable, not that they are uninformative.

records.population: Aerospace and defence maintenance documentation, originally civil aviation maintenance procedures written for non-native readers
records.version_or_commit: Issue 9, released 15 January 2025, by the ASD Simplified Technical English Maintenance Group
records.licence: unknown; the specification PDF is downloadable free from asd-ste100.org after registration, redistribution terms were not verified
records.finding: A controlled language is a different philosophy from plain language: instead of coaching writers towards clarity, it removes the choice. Issue 9 carries about fifty-three writing rules and roughly nine hundred approved words, each word constrained to one meaning and one part of speech. The decision rule this yields is that ambiguity is best attacked at the vocabulary layer, not the sentence layer, because one word with two meanings defeats any amount of sentence discipline. The cost is deliberate: the text is not idiomatic and is not meant to be.
records.applicability_limits: Built for safety-critical procedural instructions read by people whose first language is not English, under time pressure, where a misread step injures someone. It is a bad fit for explanation, persuasion, marketing or anything conceptual, and its approved-word restriction is unworkable for a fast-moving product vocabulary. The specification itself was not read for this record; the rule and dictionary counts come from the association's own pages and trade press. No controlled trial of comprehension gains was located.

records.source: Multimethods randomised trial of plain language versions of COVID-19 health recommendations for parents
records.study_design: Pragmatic, allocation-concealed, blinded, superiority randomised controlled trial with a nested qualitative component
records.population: Parents or legal guardians aged eighteen or over of a child under eighteen
records.benchmark: Understanding of the recommendation, plus preference and intended behaviour
records.version_or_commit: Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, volume 161, pages 8 to 19, September 2023; online 6 July 2023
records.licence: Elsevier copyright, paywalled; publisher landing page returned 403, abstract and indexing records only
records.finding: Against a standard-language control, a plain-language rewrite of the same recommendation improved both preference and understanding in parents. This is the strongest available evidence that plain language is not merely a taste: holding content constant and varying only the wording changed what readers took away. The design is the transferable part, an A/B of two renderings of one decision with comprehension questions as the outcome, which is a template any product can run on its own copy.
records.applicability_limits: Health recommendations under pandemic conditions, self-selected online participants, English only. Full text was not accessible, so effect size and confidence interval are not recorded here and must not be quoted. Understanding was measured by comprehension questions immediately after reading, which is not the same as acting correctly a week later.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-07, from the same programme with the same intervention type, found no significant understanding gain in a younger population.

records.source: Plain Language vs Standard Format for Youth Understanding of COVID-19 Recommendations, randomised clinical trial
records.study_design: Pragmatic, allocation-concealed, blinded, superiority randomised clinical trial with integrated qualitative interviews; 1:1 allocation
records.population: 268 analysed participants aged fifteen to twenty-four, any country with internet access, English comprehension required, 86.9 per cent from the Americas; recruited from 918 initial participants
records.benchmark: Proportion of correct responses to seven comprehension questions
records.licence: unknown; PMC open-access article, per-article licence not verified on the page
records.finding: The plain-language version produced no significant difference in understanding, mean difference 5.2 per cent, 95 per cent confidence interval minus 1.2 to 11.6, p equals 0.11, while scoring higher on accessibility, usability and satisfaction. The principle to take is that plain language buys two different goods and they come apart. It reliably makes text feel easier and reliably improves the experience of reading; whether it improves comprehension depends on the population and the baseline. Claiming the comprehension benefit without measuring it is unsupported.
records.applicability_limits: Younger, digitally literate, self-selected participants who already had high health literacy, which compresses the headroom for a comprehension gain and is the authors' own stated limitation. Uncontrolled online setting, 166 participants excluded for speeding. English only. A null result in one population is not evidence of no effect generally.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-06 found a significant understanding gain from the same intervention type in parents, and FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-01 makes understanding definitional to plainness.

records.source: W3C, Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (COGA)
records.population: Readers with cognitive and learning disabilities; authored by the W3C WAI COGA task force
records.version_or_commit: W3C Working Group Note, published 29 April 2021, non-normative, explicitly marked as a draft that may be updated or obsoleted
records.licence: W3C Document Licence (2015 copyright-software-and-document licence); paraphrase only, do not copy pattern text
records.finding: Language accessibility decomposes into checkable patterns rather than a vibe. Objective 3 gives clear words, simple tense and voice, no double negatives or nested clauses, literal language over metaphor, one instruction per step, and summaries for long documents. Objective 4 covers errors and forms: visible labels, step-by-step instructions, accept multiple input formats, avoid data loss and timeouts, give feedback, use familiar units. The decision rule worth binding is one instruction per step and no figurative language in an instruction, because both are mechanically reviewable and both defeat readers that prose-level advice does not reach.
records.applicability_limits: Explicitly supplemental and non-normative: these patterns are not WCAG conformance requirements and cannot be cited as a legal obligation. The note has not been republished since 2021 while WCAG moved to 2.2, so it is drifting out of alignment. Guidance is qualitative; almost none of it carries a pass or fail threshold. Its recommendation against figurative language conflicts with brand voice guidance that leans on idiom.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-11 and FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-12 both encourage conversational and idiomatic phrasing, which is directly the literal-language pattern's opposite.
records.review: on-change-of:W3C republishing coga-usable or folding it into WCAG 3

records.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Error Message Guidelines
records.population: General interface users; drawn from NN/g consulting practice rather than a stated study sample
records.version_or_commit: Article by Neusesser and Sunwall, published 14 May 2023
records.licence: Nielsen Norman Group copyright, all rights reserved; paraphrase only
records.finding: An error message has four separable jobs and most bad ones fail on placement, not wording. Put the message next to what caused it, mark it redundantly so colour is not the only signal, match severity to consequence, and do not fire before the user has finished. Only then does wording matter: name the problem precisely, offer the fix, and do not blame the reader. The strongest operational rule is that user input must survive the error; the message that makes someone retype is worse than the message with clumsy grammar.
records.applicability_limits: Practitioner guidance grounded in the ten heuristics rather than in studies reported alongside it, so the individual claims are expert consensus and not measured effects. Framed for graphical forms; it says little about command-line errors, API error bodies, or logs. Proprietary and all rights reserved, so nothing may be lifted verbatim into a house pack.

records.source: Unicode MessageFormat 2.0, message-format-wg and LDML Part 9
records.population: Software localisation tooling, programming languages and libraries
records.version_or_commit: Stable as of CLDR 47, released 17 April 2025; normative text published as UTS 35 (LDML) Part 9; some default functions and the u: namespace remain Draft
records.licence: Unicode Licence, per the repository LICENSE and the Unicode Terms of Use
records.finding: A translatable message is a unit with a data model, not a string with holes punched in it. MessageFormat 2.0 makes selection on plurality, gender and grammatical case part of the message itself, so a translator can add a distinction the English source never had. The binding decision rule that follows is: never build a sentence by concatenation, and never let the number of variants be fixed by the source language. Concatenation is the single i18n defect that cannot be fixed downstream by any translator.
records.applicability_limits: Stable but young in adoption; library support was still consolidating at the cutoff, and parts of the default function set are Draft, so pinning a version matters. Migration from ICU MessageFormat 1 or gettext is a real cost and is not justified for a product with one locale and no plans for a second. It solves message structure, not tone, terminology or layout.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-12 is a competing design that reached the same asymmetric-localisation conclusion years earlier with a different syntax, so the ecosystem is not settled on one format.
records.review: on-change-of:the u: namespace or default functions moving out of Draft

records.version_or_commit: cldr.unicode.org as published 2026-08-03, copyright notice 1991 to 2026
records.finding: Plural selection uses six category tags, zero, one, two, few, many and other, of which only other is mandatory. The trap the specification names explicitly is treating the category one as meaning the number one: it means any number that behaves like one in that language, which differs per locale. The rule to bind is that plural forms are looked up per locale, never derived from the English singular and plural, and that a locale's minimal pairs are not translations of the English pair.
records.applicability_limits: Covers grammatical number only. It does not solve gender, case, or the ordering of clauses, and it does not tell you how many forms a given translator will actually supply. Category coverage varies by locale and CLDR release, so a hard-coded switch on six tags is already wrong for some locales and will drift.
records.review: on-change-of:a CLDR release altering plural category coverage

records.population: Application localisation, originating in Mozilla product localisation across many locales
records.version_or_commit: Fluent Syntax 1.0, released April 2019; implementations in JavaScript, Python and Rust
records.finding: Asymmetric localisation: a translation need not have the same shape as its source. One flat English string may become a multi-variant message in another locale, and the developer does not have to anticipate that or ship a code change to permit it. The generalisable principle is that the source language must not cap the expressiveness of a translation, which reframes the whole i18n problem from string substitution to per-locale authoring.
records.applicability_limits: Syntax 1.0 has not moved since 2019 and the project is described by Mozilla as a research project, so it is stable rather than actively evolving; adopting it now is a bet against MessageFormat 2.0 becoming the ecosystem default. Three official implementations only. It carries no opinion on tone, terminology or readability.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-10 reaches the same asymmetry conclusion inside a standards process with wider intended adoption, which makes Fluent the riskier long-term choice for a new system.
records.review: on-change-of:a Fluent Syntax 2.0 or a formal deprecation in favour of MessageFormat 2.0

records.source: W3C Internationalization, Text size in translation
records.population: Interface designers translating English into European languages; expansion figures attributed to IBM globalisation guidelines
records.version_or_commit: w3.org/International article as published 2026-08-03; no version or revision date stated on the page
records.licence: W3C Document Licence per the site footer; paraphrase only, the expansion table is reproduced as figures, not as text
records.finding: Text expansion in translation is inversely related to source length. English strings of up to ten characters average two to three times longer once translated into European languages, while strings over seventy characters average about thirty per cent longer. The design consequence is that the shortest strings, which are exactly the ones in buttons, tabs and labels, are the ones most likely to break the layout. Short microcopy therefore needs the most layout slack, not the least, and fixed-width containers around single words are the highest-risk pattern.
records.applicability_limits: English to European languages only. Says nothing about CJK, which usually contracts, or about right-to-left scripts, vertical text or line-breaking. The figures are averages attributed to a third party, with no distribution or worst case given, so they size a risk rather than set a limit. Undated, which weakens it as a citation.

records.source: MicrosoftDocs/globalization, How to perform internationalization testing
records.population: Product teams shipping software in multiple locales
records.version_or_commit: main branch, file last updated 4 May 2024
records.licence: unknown; public MicrosoftDocs repository, licence file not verified for this path
records.finding: Pseudo-localisation converts a whole class of i18n defects from post-translation surprises into pre-translation test failures, at no translation cost. It catches truncation, concatenated sentences, strings never externalised, and hardcoded text. It is honest about the boundary: it cannot catch what only emerges during translation, meaning source ambiguity and terminology inconsistency. The rule this supports is that a pseudo-locale build should be a gate before any string goes to a translator, because after that point every one of these defects costs money in every locale at once.
records.applicability_limits: Detects mechanical and layout faults, not meaning. Passing a pseudo-locale run says nothing about whether the copy is understandable or correctly translated. The document is generic guidance without a runnable harness, and it has not been touched since May 2024. Its usefulness depends entirely on the i18n library already supporting a pseudo-locale.

records.source: Microsoft Writing Style Guide, Top 10 tips for style and voice
records.population: Microsoft product and documentation writers, US English
records.licence: Microsoft copyright, terms of use apply; the source repository is MicrosoftDocs/microsoft-style-guide-pr, per-file licence not verified
records.finding: A house voice is defined by a small set of rewrite operations, not by adjectives. The transferable ones are: lead with the verb, front-load keywords so a scanning reader hits them first, cut every word that is not doing work, and replace an error label with the shape of the correct input, so Invalid ID becomes a statement of what a valid ID looks like. That last example is the most reusable rule in the guide, because it turns a diagnosis into an instruction. The rest of the ten are house conventions, not principles.
records.applicability_limits: Half the tips are arbitrary house conventions, sentence case, serial comma, one space after a full stop, no spaces around dashes, and they conflict directly with other defensible house styles including this repository's own voice law, which forbids em-dashes outright. US English throughout. Proprietary, so it is a reference for the shape of a style guide, not a source to copy from. It is a style guide, not evidence: no comprehension data supports any of the ten.
records.counter_evidence: FRAG-WRITING-CONTENT-08 warns against idiom and figurative language, while write like you speak and project friendliness push towards contractions and conversational idiom.

records.population: Mailchimp writers, published for reuse by other organisations
records.version_or_commit: styleguide.mailchimp.com as published 2026-08-03; no version number given
records.licence: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International; attribution to Mailchimp required, commercial reuse not permitted
records.finding: The structural contribution is the split between voice and tone: voice is fixed and describes who the product is, tone varies by the reader's emotional state at that moment. That gives a decision rule with teeth, because it says the same product should sound different in a celebration screen and in a failed-payment error, and it forces a writer to ask what the reader is feeling before choosing words. The guide also treats Writing About People as a first-class section rather than an appendix, which is the right weight for the decisions most likely to cause harm.
records.applicability_limits: The NonCommercial clause is load-bearing: a commercial product cannot adopt this text into its own style guide, only read it and write its own. It is one company's marketing-led voice, and the guide states it breaks grammar rules for preference, so it should be read as a worked example of the form, not as a rulebook. No evidence that tone-matching improves any outcome; the claim is asserted.
